newsitem.title: USA: Japan must avoid big rise in trade surplus - Rubin.
newsitem.headline: Japan must avoid big rise in trade surplus - Rubin.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on Wednesday urged Japan to maintain strong domestic demand and avoid a big rise in its trade surplus, calling that "critical" to the economic outlook in Asia.

"Japan faces an important challenge in sustaining the conditions for strong domestic demand-led growth and avoiding a significant increase in the current account surplus," Rubin said in a speech for delivery here to the New York Stock Exchange Board of Directors.
He said Japan also faces additional challenges in strengthening its financial institutions.

"How it deals with these challenges is of critical importance to the economic outlook in Asia," Rubin said. "Like the United States, Japan's trading partners have much to gain from increased access to Japan's markets, a stable financial system and strong domestic demand led growth."

Rubin said he was encouraged by the progress that Japan has made in recent years in reducing its surplus and he welcomed Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's commitment to further reform and deregulation.
Rubin sets off on Thursday for a six-day trip to Asia. His first stop is Tokyo on Friday, where he will meet Hashimoto.
During his six-day trip, Rubin will also visit the Philippines for a meeting of Asia-Pacific finance ministers and Vietnam.
"Our goal is clear -- to foster growth in Asia, which will, in turn, promote global growth," he said. "The end result will be increased U.S. exports ... and greater prosperity."

He said he expects to reach an agreement in the Philippines with fellow ministers from the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation group on a set of principles to guide development of capital markets and enhance the role of the private sector in financing infrastructure construction.
Rubin said he will also seek APEC support for a successful conclusion of World Trade Organization negotiations to open up the financial services industry to more competition.
Washington wants to strike a deal by the end of this year. But for that to occur, key emerging markets must significantly improve on their offers of increased access, Rubin said.
The Treasury chief will be the highest-ranking U.S. economic policymaker to visit Vitenam in decades.

"The United States, in both the government and the private sector, has much to offer to promote growth in Vietnam," Rubin said. But, he added, Vietnam must press ahead with reforms and be willing to open up its markets substantially in return.
